new_statements.quote: Stress is indicated by a greater degree of force in the production of a syllable, a noticeably higher pitch than in unstressed syllables, and some degree of lengthening. In general, primary stress falls on the only syllable of monosyllabic words or on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words. Examples of antepenultimate stress are extremely rare, e.g. ['ttjbtit] 'we defecate'. Final stress in polysyllables is more frequent, but is generally restricted to a few loan words, e.g. [a'had] 'Sunday, week' (< Arabic), and some polymorphemic verb forms with monosyllabic roots, e.g. [na'pe] 'he does' from ['pe] 'to do'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of polysyllables (and on the only syllable of monosyllables). Antepenultimate stress is extremely rare; final stress occurs in a few loans (ahád 'Sunday') and in some polymorphemic verb forms built on monosyllabic roots (napé 'he does' from pé).
new_statements.exceptions: Extremely rare antepenultimate stress (the text garbles the IPA of the one example; it corresponds to orthographic tciotit 'we defecate' in the transcribed passage on p. 57); final stress in a few loanwords (ahád < Arabic) and in some polymorphemic verb forms with monosyllabic roots (napé 'he does').
new_statements.identity_note: Taba = East Makian = Makian Dalam / Makian Timur / Inner Makian (Bowden 2001: 1, 'The Taba language has generally been referred to in the literature as either East Makian, Makian Timur, Inner Makian or Makian Dalam'). Both statements describe the Waikyon (Indonesian: Ngofakiaha) village dialect on Makian island; Bowden 2001 (§2.8) notes that other villages (Tahane, Mailoa, Ngelo) differ in a few segments (o vs a, mostly in stressed vowels) and in glide/stress shifts in individual words, not in the stress rule.

new_statements.quote: Primary stress in Taba falls on the penultimate syllable of a word, unless the word is monosyllabic, in which case it falls on the only syllable of the word. In words of four or five syllables, secondary stress occurs on the preantepenultimate syllable. There are no words in my corpus of more than five syllables, and words of more than three syllables are quite rare. Stress is never affected by affixation. A few exceptions to these generalisations occur: some disyllabic words have lexical stress on the final syllable, e.g. amseh 'be drunk', magun 'be silent', mak6t 'red'.

new_statements.relation_note: Confirms the catalog placement exactly and supplies the secondary-stress pattern that the catalog's binary string encodes (1010, 01010 = preantepenultimate secondary in 4- and 5-syllable words); the catalog's 6-, 7- and 8-syllable strings go beyond Bowden's corpus, which has no words over five syllables. Description is of the Waikyon (Ngofakiaha) dialect, Makian island.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable (on the only syllable in monosyllables); in four- and five-syllable words a secondary stress falls on the preantepenultimate syllable, i.e. two syllables to the left of the primary (1010, 01010). Stress is assigned per surface vowel (vowel sequences are separate syllables, no diphthongs) and is unaffected by affixation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the preantepenultimate syllable in words of four or five syllables (examples (47)-(48), (49)-(50), pp. 52-53, e.g. [sakoamu] with secondary on the first and primary on the third syllable; [kamkumpappido] 'large woven rice basket' five syllables). No words longer than five syllables in the corpus. Glide replacement of the third vowel of a quadrisyllable removes the secondary stress from the first syllable (§2.5.2, ex. (71)).
new_statements.exceptions: A few disyllables with lexical final stress (amséh 'be drunk', magún 'be silent', makót 'red' -- the text drops the acute accents; 'mak6t' = makót), historically *ma- derived forms; the causative prefix ha- attracts stress only in its intensifying function (ex. (52) tahasak); affixes and clitics never bear stress, particles do; full lexical reduplications carry primary stress twice; enclitic Undergoer pronouns lose stress; cliticisation can reassign stress (mawoappo 'the next day'); sporadic glide replacement kiu ~ kju shifts stress to the following vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: Taba = East Makian = Makian Dalam / Makian Timur / Inner Makian (Bowden 2001: 1, 'The Taba language has generally been referred to in the literature as either East Makian, Makian Timur, Inner Makian or Makian Dalam'). Both statements describe the Waikyon (Indonesian: Ngofakiaha) village dialect on Makian island; Bowden 2001 (§2.8) notes that other villages (Tahane, Mailoa, Ngelo) differ in a few segments (o vs a, mostly in stressed vowels) and in glide/stress shifts in individual words, not in the stress rule.

audit.recode_to: No class change. Optional refinement of the domain note: Bowden 2001 says affixes and clitics never bear stress and 'affixation never affects stress' (§2.4 p. 53 ex. (51) ha-ˈmul, not *ˈhamul; §3.1.3 pp. 89-90; ch. 11 p. 274 demonstratives iˈne, siˈne, iˈda with unstressed prefixes), and Bowden & Hajek 1996:56 give [naˈpe] < [ˈpe]. So penultimate stress is computed on the root/stem; suffixation (-o, -ma, with unstressed-vowel deletion) keeps the penult surface-true, but prefixed or procliticised monosyllabic roots surface with word-final stress. If the catalog's domain field distinguishes word from STEM, STEM (root + suffixes, prefixes extrametrical) is the more faithful value; lexical final-stress exceptions (amseh, magun, makót; loans like aˈhad) could be noted under exceptions.
audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Bowden 2001 PDF we hold text at p. 51 §2.4, exactly as the locator says. Deciding source is a modern 451-page reference grammar (Pacific Linguistics 521, 2001; = 1997 PhD) with a dedicated stress section giving primary penultimate stress, secondary stress on the pre-antepenult in 4-5 syllable words, phonetic correlates, and exceptions; this is the top item in Glottolog's descriptive bibliography (all three entries are Bowden's own works) and we hold it in full. The one additional source located, the JIPA Illustration Bowden & Hajek 1996 (downloaded to, independently states the same penultimate rule (p. 56) and adds the exception classes, so it confirms the fixed-penultimate coding and the stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable) rule string.
